transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-05-20
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~70 minutes
Attendees: Jamie Liu (Redwood AE), Carlos Mendez (Redwood SE), Priya Shah (Redwood Infra), Alex Torres (Nimbus CTO), Maya Gupta (Nimbus ML Infra), Jordan Lee (Nimbus Platform)

Summary (auto-generated, may be imperfect): team reviewed recurring OOMs and timeouts seen on Nimbus testbed, discussed CUDA driver mismatches, KV cache pressure, batching impacts, and retry semantics. Agreed on repro artifacts and next steps.

Transcript:
[00:00] Jamie Liu: hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. quick agenda — reproduce OOMs, root-cause hypotheses (cuda, kernel, kv cache), and retry/backoff semantics. carlos will run through logs.
[00:18] Carlos Mendez: cool, i'll share my screen — i pulled a few recent traces from the nimbus sandbox. quick note, the transcriptions are from our internal run, so some names may be off. the first one is a 32GB A100 host; we see OOMs at ~token 1024 during a long context generation.
[00:36] Maya Gupta: yes we've seen it across batches, more often when we push concurrent sessions (50-100 qps). latency spikes first then OOM in cudaMalloc.
[00:45] Carlos Mendez: right — stack shows cudaErrorMemoryAllocation, then driver complaining about out-of-memory on device 0. interestingly, the process memory on host isn't that high, it's GPU memory fragmentation and kv cache growth.
[01:05] Jordan Lee: to be clear, these are raw generation calls through your hosted endpoint or dedicated?
[01:12] Alex Torres: currently hitting Redwood Hosted API in our sandbox account, not Dedicated yet, but we're exploring Dedicated after these stability bits.
[01:22] Priya Shah: one hypothesis — continuous batching + KV cache retention keeps per-session KV state; if clients pin very long contexts or don't signal end-of-session, kv cache inflates and we run out. also quantization mismatch can increase scratch memory.
[01:40] Maya Gupta: we do pin long histories for chat — up to 8k tokens — and we have variable sequence lengths. we thought your runtime prunes cold sessions but maybe our TTL is too long.
[01:52] Carlos Mendez: our TTL defaults are conservative for Hosted; for Dedicated customers TTL can be tuned. i'll show you the kv cache eviction logic.
[02:03] [Carlos shares pseudo-config]: kv_cache_ttl_seconds: 3600, max_sessions_per_gpu: 200, batcher_max_seq: 4096
[02:18] Carlos Mendez: so in this config, if many sessions have long histories, the kv cache can exceed memory. when combined with peak batching (batcher tries to merge multi-session requests), it spikes transient memory. that's where we see cudaMalloc failures.
[02:35] Maya Gupta: makes sense. is there a diagnostics flag we can enable to surface kv cache size per-session?
[02:40] Priya Shah: yes, there's a per-session telemetry: kv_bytes_retained and kv_last_access. we can surface that in trace logs — i'll add an annotation to the replay.
[02:52] Jordan Lee: what about timeouts? some of our requests hit 30s and then client retries, which sometimes causes duplicate inflight work and doubles memory usage.
[03:03] Carlos Mendez: that's a common pattern — client-side blind retries during long tail cause concurrent duplicates; without idempotency tokens, each retry is treated as new and can lead to two simultaneous KV allocations.
[03:14] Alex Torres: so what's the best practice for retries? backoff? idempotency tokens?
[03:19] Priya Shah: recommended: exponential backoff + jitter on the client, and include an idempotency token or request-id header we can use to collapse duplicate requests server-side. in Hosted we do best-effort de-duplication if request-id matches within a window. for Dedicated we can configure stricter dedupe policies.
[03:38] Maya Gupta: we do send a request-id but it's not consistently unique across our proxies — we'll fix that.
[03:45] Carlos Mendez: another nuance: some kernels allocate transient workspace memory (attention scratch) that scales with batch_size x seq_len x head_dim. if attention kernel version is suboptimal for the quantized model, workspace can blow up.
[04:05] Jamie Liu: can you expand on quantization mismatches? we saw a customer earlier where FP16 vs 8-bit kernels had different workspace needs.
[04:15] Carlos Mendez: sure — certain fused kernels for int8/4 need additional unpack/pack buffers, and some heuristics in the runtime allocate temporary buffers to convert between representations. if the runtime picked a conservative kernel (older cuda arch fallback), memory goes up. driver/kernel mismatch can cause fallback to generic kernels.
[04:36] Alex Torres: could driver versions cause this? we run different node pools with slightly different drivers.
[04:42] Priya Shah: absolutely — we saw a case where a mismatched NVIDIA driver + runtime combo caused kernel fallbacks that doubled transient memory. that's why we recommend matched driver/container images. we'll share the exact driver matrix we test against.
[04:58] Jordan Lee: we also saw sporadic CUDA illegal instruction errors in one pool. logs show CUDART illegal instruction and container OOMs.
[05:10] Carlos Mendez: illegal instruction usually indicates a mismatch between compiled kernels and GPU ISA (sm_ versions). older drivers may fail to run newer kernels. those lead to process crashes and restarts — which show up as timeouts and cascade retries.
[05:27] Jamie Liu: ok recapping root causes so far: kv cache blowup from long-lived sessions + batching duplicates from client retries, kernel/workspace inflation from quantization + driver/kernel mismatch, and driver/container mismatch causing illegal instruction/crash.
[05:44] Alex Torres: correct. what about timeouts at the LB layer? we saw 15s timeouts on our side sometimes.
[05:51] Carlos Mendez: there are two timeout layers: load-balancer/client side, and internal per-request SLO. if LB timeout triggers first and client retries, it's the duplicated pattern again. we can coordinate on LB timeouts while we optimize tail latency.
[06:05] Maya Gupta: any immediate mitigations we can apply without changing client code?
[06:10] Priya Shah: server side we can tighten KV TTL, reduce max sessions per GPU, and lower batcher concurrency temporarily. we can also enable request dedupe window to collapse inflight duplicates if request-id header present.
[06:25] Jordan Lee: can we do that on Hosted?
[06:28] Carlos Mendez: yes for sandbox accounts we can flip those flags; for production we suggest testing in Dedicated where you can set hardened configs.
[06:37] Maya Gupta: about retries — what are Redwood's default retry semantics? like how many retries and exponential backoff?
[06:45] Jamie Liu: default is 3 retries with a small exponential backoff (100ms base) for transient 5xx errors; for timeouts we recommend client implement 2-3 retries with backoff and include idempotency. but again, blind retries can make things worse.
[07:02] Carlos Mendez: important: our runtime returns a 202 for queued work when throttled; client should interpret 202 as queued and not necessarily retry aggressively.
[07:13] Alex Torres: about observability, we need flamegraphs and memory histograms to correlate spikes.
[07:20] Priya Shah: we can instrument per-GPU memory watermark metrics and produce a flamegraph of per-stage allocations (kv, workspace, cache). i'll include a sample in the runbook.
[07:30] [15 minute mark omitted — call continues diving into log excerpts]
[22:05] Carlos Mendez: pasted log snippet: "W runtime: cudaMalloc failed 0x60000000 size= 1.2GB align=256" then "E model: OOM while allocating attention_workspace" then "I eviction: evicting session id abc123 (last access 2h) reclaimed 1.8GB"
[22:34] Jordan Lee: interesting eviction happened after OOM attempt. is eviction synchronous?
[22:38] Carlos Mendez: eviction is opportunistic; we try to evict cold sessions before new allocation but if allocation comes first, OOM happens, then eviction kicks in — that ordering can cause transient failures. we should pre-emptively check estimated alloc + current free and proactively evict if below threshold.
[22:55] Priya Shah: yes, we have a fix on the branch that adds pre-allocation checks and a soft-guard that triggers eviction with a lock to avoid races. it reduces OOMs in stress tests.
[23:08] Maya Gupta: will that add latency?
[23:11] Priya Shah: small microsecond-level stalls but avoids multi-second retries. tradeoff is worth it.
[23:20] Carlos Mendez: another pattern: when quantized models hit long sequences, we observed wrong workspace estimate leading to cudaMalloc returning ENOMEM because estimate left out extra conversion buffers. runtime now has a new path that computes conservative workspace for quantized int8 flows.
[23:36] Alex Torres: can you run a small repro with our payload? we can sanitize and upload to the S3 path you provide.
[23:43] Jamie Liu: yes — we'll provide a minimal repro template and a sanitized sample S3 path: https://s3.redwood-internal/test-repro/nimbus-ooms. please include request-id and timestamps.
[23:56] Jordan Lee: also concerning were timeouts combined with retry causing double allocation. any server-side dedupe window length?
[24:04] Carlos Mendez: default is 30s dedupe window for request-id matches; if a retry hits within that window we collapse. we'll increase to 60s for your sandbox. note: collapse requires identical request payloads (hash match).
[24:20] Maya Gupta: what happens to in-flight deduped requests from different clients that omit request-id?
[24:25] Priya Shah: without request-id we can't safely dedupe; we can detect approximate duplicates by payload hash but it's probabilistic and costly. best is to enforce request-id at proxy layer.
[24:38] Alex Torres: ok that's actionable.
[24:42] Carlos Mendez: on the illegal-instruction side, we need to map node pools to driver/kernel combos. can you provide the nodepool identifiers?
[24:50] Jordan Lee: yes, pool-a-driver-520.61, pool-b-driver-470.142, pool-c-driver-535.86.
[24:59] Priya Shah: pool-b's older 470 driver likely caused kernel fallback/illegal instruction on some newer kernels compiled for sm_8X. we'll recommend aligning to the tested set (we'll share exact matrix).
[25:11] Carlos Mendez: quick remediation plan we discussed: 1) toggle kv TTL lower in sandbox, 2) increase dedupe window + require request-id, 3) tighten batcher concurrency cap, 4) reproduce with sanitized payloads uploaded to S3, 5) run Dedicated test with matching driver image.
[25:35] Maya Gupta: timeline?
[25:37] Jamie Liu: we'll do items 1-3 this week, help reproduce (item 4) by Friday, and schedule Dedicated baseline test early next week.
[25:45] [Later — detailed Q&A on retry semantics]
[30:05] Jordan Lee: on retried completions, how do you ensure token dedupe? if a retry yields partial tokens before client cancels, we sometimes get duplicate output.
[30:18] Carlos Mendez: token-level dedupe is hard; our approach is request-level idempotency. for partial completions we return a stream and include a final status with sequence id; clients should cancel inflight on receiving final or resume from checkpoint. for exactly-once generation you need a combination of idempotency and monotonic output markers.
[30:40] Maya Gupta: is there a recommended header/pattern we should implement?
[30:44] Priya Shah: yes — include x-request-id and x-client-session; include a resume token for long polling. we can share a sample SDK pattern.
[30:55] Alex Torres: any change to cost when enabling KV TTL lower or turning on dedupe?
[30:59] Carlos Mendez: lowering TTL reduces memory and cost; dedupe reduces duplicate work so reduces cost. however, enabling aggressive eviction may increase latency for resumed sessions hitting cache miss. it's a cost/latency tradeoff.
[31:15] Jamie Liu: final part — what logs and artifacts do we need from Nimbus to diagnose further?
[31:20] Carlos Mendez: please provide: request-ids + timestamps for failing requests, sanitized payloads (or small repro), per-node GPU driver versions, and any kube/container runtime logs around the failure windows. upload to the S3 path.
[31:33] Maya Gupta: we'll compile that.
[31:35] Jamie Liu: ok let's capture the explicit next steps — i will read them out.
[31:40] Jamie Liu: 1) Redwood toggle TTL+dedupe in sandbox; 2) Nimbus to upload repro and logs; 3) Redwood SE will run repro on Dedicated image with tested driver; 4) follow-up deep dive for retry semantics next week.
[31:55] Alex Torres: agreed. thanks.
[32:00] [call ends]

Notes/Artifacts referenced:
- KB/runbook link (will be shared): https://redwood.app/s/runbooks/gpu-oom-diagnostics
- Sandbox S3 repro path: https://s3.redwood-internal/test-repro/nimbus-ooms (redwood request: please include request-ids)
- Driver compatibility matrix (to be shared): https://redwood.app/s/compat/driver-matrix

Observations (SE/Infra):
- High likelihood that a combination of long-lived sessions + client retries caused duplicate KV allocations that pushed transient GPU memory above threshold.
- Quantization and kernel selection can increase workspace allocation; driver mismatch can cause fallback to generic kernels that need more memory or fail with illegal instruction.
- Eviction currently opportunistic; adding pre-allocation checks and a locking eviction reduces races and OOMs (small latency tradeoff).
- Deduplication with request-id recommended to avoid duplicate inflight allocation.

End of transcript.
